claims.text: Superconductivity in high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by enhanced electron–phonon coupling.
Chemical disorder induces local lattice distortions that mediate enhanced electron–phonon coupling.
Randomly distributed constituent elements produce significant chemical disorder.
Random elemental distributions produce local lattice distortions and strain fields.
Reducing the number of constituent elements systematically lowers chemical disorder.
Disorder-induced lattice distortions enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Increased electron–phonon coupling elevates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Increased electron–phonon coupling strengthens Cooper-pair formation.
The proposed changes in electron–phonon coupling affect superconducting critical temperature.
The proposed changes in electron–phonon coupling affect superconducting gap structure.
Higher-disorder alloys will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than comparable lower-disorder alloys.
Higher-disorder alloys will exhibit modified superconducting-gap characteristics relative to lower-disorder alloys.
A fewer-element, more ordered baseline is expected to have lower electron–phonon coupling.
Lower electron–phonon coupling in the baseline is expected to produce a lower superconducting critical temperature.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to high-entropy alloys in which phonon-mediated pairing is dominant.
The proposed relationship may fail when magnetic or other electronic pairing interactions dominate.
The supplied evidence base contains no direct evidence connecting disorder-induced lattice distortion to enhanced electron–phonon coupling in high-entropy alloys.
Alternative superconducting pairing mechanisms could influence the observations.
The comparison is intended to hold lattice parameters, pressure, and environmental conditions similar while varying disorder.
A lack of statistically significant changes in superconducting properties or electron–phonon-coupling indicators with enhanced disorder would falsify the hypothesis.
